acalypha-australis.summary: Asian copperleaf is an upright annual with toothed, egg-shaped leaves that may show coppery or reddish new growth. Its small flowers sit inside broad, heart-shaped bracts, a useful distinction from several similar native copperleaf species. It grows in gardens, landscaped ground, and crop fields, and can be difficult to identify confidently before flowering, so the bracts deserve a closer look.

sources.label: Iowa State University Extension: Asian copperleaf

ocinebrellus-inornatus.summary: Asian drill snail is a small marine predator that lives among gravel, mud, and shells, often in shallow oyster beds. Also called the Japanese oyster drill, it eats oysters and other shelled animals, including mussels, clams, and barnacles. Oyster transfers have carried it beyond its northwest Pacific home, making this inconspicuous snail important to both shellfish growers and people restoring native oyster habitat.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Ocinebrellus inornatus

cyperus-microiria.summary: Asian flatsedge is a tufted annual sedge with three-sided stems and narrow leaves folded into a shallow V. Its spreading flower clusters contain slender spikelets with brown to golden scales and green centers. It grows on disturbed ground and muddy river or ditch margins; looking closely at those small spikelets is more useful for identification than treating every grasslike plant at a wet edge as a grass.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Cyperus microiria
University of Trieste: Cyperus microiria

undaria-pinnatifida.summary: Asian kelp, also known as wakame, is a large brown seaweed with a distinct central rib and, when mature, a ruffled reproductive structure near the base. It can attach to natural surfaces as well as boat hulls, ropes, and other marine equipment. Fast growth and broad blades let dense stands shade smaller algae, while its resemblance to native kelps makes careful identification worthwhile.

sources.label: Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council: Asian kelp identification card

asian-longhorned-beetle.summary: Asian longhorned beetle attacks maples and other hardwood trees, spending its immature life tunneling inside the wood. Round exit holes and coarse, sawdust-like material around a trunk or branch are useful signs to notice. The hidden feeding damage can weaken limbs even while a tree still looks healthy, which is why an unusual beetle or fresh holes in a familiar shade tree deserve attention.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Asian longhorned beetle

assiminea-parasitologica.summary: Asian marsh snail is a tiny brown snail, about five millimeters tall, with a rounded cone-shaped shell. It lives high in salt and brackish tidal marshes rather than in the deeper water many people associate with marine snails. Smithsonian researchers describe introduced Oregon populations but no observed ecological impacts there; possible competition with native marsh animals remains a concern to investigate, rather than an established outcome.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Assiminea parasitologica

limnophila-sessiliflora.summary: Asian marshweed changes its appearance at the waterline: submerged leaves are finely divided and feathery, while the leaves above water are firmer and toothed. Small pink, violet, or bluish flowers appear on exposed stems. This fast-growing aquatic perennial can regrow from fragments and form thick stands through the water column, shading other plants and interfering with canals or recreation where it becomes abundant.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Limnophila sessiliflora

brassica-tournefortii.summary: Asian mustard, often called Sahara mustard, is a winter annual that can finish its life cycle within a few months. It grows in disturbed places but also enters desert dunes, washes, shrublands, and other open habitats. Its spread through parts of southwestern North America shows why a seasonal mustard patch can matter beyond a roadside: this species is capable of moving into natural vegetation as well.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Sahara mustard

colubrina-asiatica.summary: Asian nakedwood, also called latherleaf, is a scrambling evergreen shrub whose long branches climb through surrounding vegetation. Look for shiny, broadly oval leaves with toothed edges, small greenish flowers, and rounded, capsule-like fruits. Its climbing branches can reach roughly thirty feet, so a plant that begins as a low shrub can become a substantial tangle among neighboring plants in warm coastal landscapes.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Colubrina asiatica

pachycondyla-chinensis.summary: Asian needle ant is a slender, dark ant with lighter legs and mouthparts, often nesting in damp leaf litter, rotting logs, or beneath stones. It feeds on termites and other small animals and can occupy forests as well as yards and buildings. Its sting and its ability to displace native ants make it worth recognizing; newer references usually call it Brachyponera chinensis.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension: Asian needle ant
Virginia Tech Extension: Asian needle ant

clitoria-ternatea.summary: Asian pigeonwings, more often called butterfly pea, is a twining vine with large blue to violet flowers that stand out against its green foliage. The flowers give way to flattened seedpods, revealing its membership in the pea family. It grows as a perennial in warm climates and is often cultivated elsewhere as an annual, so climate and growing conditions help explain whether it persists outdoors.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox: Clitoria ternatea

dichondra-micrantha.summary: Asian ponysfoot is a low, spreading plant associated with lawns and other closely trimmed ground. Its small flowers are easily overlooked, while the nearly hairless foliage helps distinguish it from some related dichondras. It has been planted as a lawn substitute in warm places; because similar species and misapplied names complicate identification, an unfamiliar patch is best examined beyond its overall carpetlike appearance.

sources.label: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Dichondra micrantha, drawing on Flora of New Zealand

hemigrapsus-sanguineus.summary: Asian shore crab is a small crab with a roughly square shell and three teeth along each front side. It often shelters among rocks in the intertidal zone, where the shore is alternately covered and exposed by tides. A flexible diet and competition with other shore animals have helped it change some invaded Atlantic coastal communities, making rocky shoreline surveys particularly useful for tracking it.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Hemigrapsus sanguineus

phakopsora-pachyrhizi.summary: Asian soybean rust is a fungal disease whose spores can travel on the wind between susceptible plants. The fungus needs living host tissue and can also persist on kudzu, linking a familiar vine with crop disease monitoring. Heavy infection reduces a soybean plant's ability to fill pods and seeds, so finding rust is about understanding the condition of a crop as well as identifying a leaf symptom.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension: Asian soybean rust

arivela-viscosa.summary: Asian spiderflower is an annual herb with sticky hairs, yellow flowers, and leaves usually divided into five narrow leaflets. Long, slender seed capsules follow the flowers, giving the plant another useful identifying feature. Often listed as Cleome viscosa in botanical references, it can be encountered in disturbed places; checking the leaflets and capsules helps connect those different names to the same plant.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Arivela viscosa
Flora of North America: Arivela viscosa

monopterus-albus.summary: Asian swamp eel is an elongated freshwater fish that often hides in soft sediment or narrow crevices and feeds at night. Its diet can include small fish, crayfish, insects, and other aquatic animals. The name Monopterus albus has been applied to a complex of closely related populations, so identification matters when interpreting records or studying how these predators affect an invaded wetland.

sources.label: USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Asian swamp eel
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: Asian swamp eel risk summary

nephrolepis-brownii.summary: Asian swordfern has tall fronds lined with overlapping leaflets whose tips are relatively blunt. Dark brown scales at the base of the fronds help distinguish it from similar native swordferns. It grows densely in shaded, well-drained places and disperses by windborne spores; where it forms thick stands, it can cover other plants and limit the growth of native vegetation underneath.

sources.label: University of South Florida: Florida Invasive Plants, Nephrolepis brownii

schyzocotyle-acheilognathi.summary: Asian tapeworm is a parasite of freshwater fish, particularly members of the carp and minnow family. Infected fish can carry it to new waters, including through the movement of baitfish. The worm competes for nutrients inside its host and can impair growth, with young fish especially vulnerable, so a small, hidden parasite can matter to both fish conservation and the movement of live fish.

sources.label: USGS: Asian fish tapeworm detection study
USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Asian tapeworm

aedes-albopictus.summary: Asian tiger mosquito is a daytime biter often active in the early morning and late afternoon. It breeds in small water-holding containers, including discarded tires, flowerpots, and buckets, which can bring its life cycle close to homes. The international movement of used tires helped transport this mosquito beyond Asia, illustrating how a little trapped water can carry an organism a very long way.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian tiger mosquito

penaeus-monodon.summary: Asian tiger shrimp is a large marine shrimp marked by alternating dark and pale bands across its body. Young shrimp move into estuaries, while adults return to the sea to spawn. Widely raised in aquaculture outside its Indo-Pacific home, it has escaped into other coastal waters; potential competition and disease transfer are concerns, but those possibilities should not be mistaken for proven impacts everywhere it appears.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Penaeus monodon

elatine-ambigua.summary: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping aquatic herb that forms patches on wet mud in places such as river margins and rice fields. Its small leaves and flowers make it easy to miss, and it closely resembles other waterworts. Flower stalks that bend backward in fruit are a useful clue, although submerged plants can be difficult to separate reliably from the similar Elatine triandra.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Elatine ambigua
Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB: Elatine ambigua
Rosman and colleagues (2016): New records of Elatine ambigua

corbicula-fluminea.summary: Asiatic clam is a small, sturdy bivalve with conspicuous concentric ridges across its rounded to triangular shell. It draws water through its body and filters suspended food, making dense populations an active part of a waterway's food web. Shell color varies, and scientists are still resolving species boundaries within Corbicula, so records filed under this familiar name may cover more diversity than the label suggests.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Conservation: Asian clam
USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Corbicula fluminea

commelina-communis.summary: Asiatic dayflower is easiest to notice when its two large blue petals open above a much smaller white petal. Each flower is short-lived, but the smooth, narrow leaves provide another clue: they wrap around the stem in a sheath rather than attaching by a leaf stalk. Those leaves can make a nonflowering plant resemble smartweed at a glance, so the brief blue bloom is especially helpful.

sources.label: Iowa State University Extension: Asiatic dayflower

rumex-confertus.summary: Asiatic dock grows from a basal cluster of large leaves and sends upright stems above them. It can spread both by seed and by vegetative growth, and occurs in habitats including grassland, river margins, and disturbed ground. Dense patches may shade neighboring vegetation, although their formation depends on local conditions; its size and expanding leaf clusters are more useful to notice than assuming every dock behaves alike.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Weed risk assessment for Rumex confertus

maladera-formosae.summary: Asiatic garden beetle is a small cinnamon-brown scarab, roughly the size and shape of a coffee bean. Adults feed on many garden and crop plants at night, while their pale grubs live underground and eat roots. This split life cycle explains why foliage damage and root injury may have the same cause, even when the beetles are hard to find during the day.

sources.label: University of Maine Extension: Asiatic garden beetle

striga-asiatica.summary: Asiatic witchweed is a small, stiff-stemmed flowering plant with coarse hairs and narrow green leaves. Its modest appearance hides a damaging habit: it attaches directly to the roots of grasses, including crops such as corn, sorghum, and rice, and takes water and nutrients from them. Tiny, dustlike seeds add to its persistence and spread, making the underground relationship as important as the visible flowers.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Witchweed biology and eradication program assessment

crioceris-asparagi.summary: Asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle with pale spots, often found feeding on asparagus spears and foliage. Its elongated eggs stand in rows on the plant, and the plump grayish larvae also feed there before pupating in soil. Unlike the orange spotted asparagus beetle, this species can directly spoil the edible spears, so noticing which beetle is present helps explain the kind of damage.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Vegetable Entomology: Asparagus beetle

asparagus-densiflorus.summary: Asparagus fern looks soft and feathery, but it is a flowering relative of garden asparagus rather than a true fern. Its fine green foliage is mostly modified stems, while the true leaves are tiny scales; mature plants can produce small flowers and red berries. Cultivated widely in containers and warm gardens, it can spread through bird-carried seeds, so the delicate appearance conceals a durable plant.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Extension: Asparagus fern

phyllonorycter-apparella.summary: Aspen leaf blotch miner is a tiny moth whose caterpillars live between the surfaces of aspen and cottonwood leaves. Their feeding makes blotched patches, and silk drawn across a leaf can shrink into a raised ridge over the mine. The early larvae feed on sap before eating leaf tissue, so an affected leaf records several stages of an insect's life even when the moth is never seen.

sources.label: Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks: Aspen leaf blotch miner

conyza-bonariensis.summary: Asthmaweed, also called hairy fleabane, is a rapidly growing annual or biennial of cultivated fields and other disturbed ground. It occurs in settings from orchards and nurseries to roadsides and canal banks, where it competes with neighboring plants for water. Because it can be confused with horseweed, its scientific name is useful when comparing identification guides or discussing an unfamiliar fleabane in a field.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Hairy fleabane

conyza-floribunda.summary: This asthmaweed is an upright herb with narrow leaves and many small flower heads on branches concentrated toward the top. The tiny fruits carry white bristles, and flowering typically extends from summer into fall in the Flora of North America account. It grows in disturbed places, but its tangled naming history makes careful identification worthwhile: botanical references have treated it differently from other closely related fleabanes.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Conyza floribunda
USDA GRIN: Conyza floribunda taxonomy
Singhurst and Holmes (2013): Conyza floribunda in Texas

tamarix-aphylla.summary: Athel tamarisk is an evergreen shrub or large tree whose minute leaves hug slender, jointed twigs. Clusters of tiny pink to white flowers soften its otherwise fine-textured crown. A deep taproot helps it endure dry conditions, and it tolerates saline or alkaline soils; those traits explain its use in harsh landscapes, while the twiglike foliage helps distinguish it from many ordinary shade trees.

sources.label: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Tamarix aphylla

hedera-hibernica.summary: Atlantic ivy, often called Irish ivy, is an evergreen vine with waxy leaves that can form a thick groundcover and climb surrounding trees or structures. Established vines spread across the ground, and broken stem pieces can start new plants. Birds also carry seeds from the berries, helping explain how a planted ivy patch can extend into nearby woodland and cover other vegetation.

sources.label: Oregon State University: Ivy

aleuroclava-aucubae.summary: Aucuba whitefly feeds on a surprisingly broad range of trees and shrubs, including aucuba, ivy, citrus, mulberry, and several ornamental plants. Infested plant material can move it between places, making nursery and landscape observations useful. California's 2022 assessment found no reported plant damage or significant economic effects, so its presence should be distinguished from evidence that it is harming the plant on which it was found.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Aleuroclava aucubae assessment

geranium-homeanum.summary: Australasian geranium is a low, sprawling herb with coarse hairs and rounded leaves divided into several lobes. Small pink to nearly white flowers usually appear in pairs, and its fleshy taproot supports growth that may last more than one season. In its Australian habitat it favors damp forest sites and rainforest margins, offering a useful habitat clue alongside the leaf shape and paired flowers.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Geranium homeanum

aedes-notoscriptus.summary: Australian backyard mosquito is a dark mosquito with banded legs, a pale ring around its feeding tube, and fine pale markings forming a lyre shape on its back. Its larvae use natural water pockets such as tree holes as well as rain-filled tires, gutters, and plant trays. That flexibility ties its life cycle closely to the small water-holding spaces people create around homes.

sources.label: Northern Territory Department of Health: Common mosquitoes, Aedes notoscriptus

pteris-tremula.summary: Australian brake is a fern with finely divided fronds ending in long, narrow segments. Its spore-bearing structures run along the underside margins, protected by the rolled leaf edges. It grows in varied sheltered places, including forest margins, streambanks, and gardens, so looking underneath a frond can reveal more about its identity than the soft, feathery outline alone.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Pteris tremula

pittosporum-undulatum.summary: Australian cheesewood is a small tree with glossy leaves whose edges form gentle waves. Fragrant white flowers are followed by rounded yellow-orange fruits that open to expose sticky orange seeds. Birds help disperse those seeds, connecting a familiar planted tree with new seedlings nearby; the combination of wavy foliage, scented flowers, and opening fruit is especially useful when recognizing it through the seasons.

sources.label: Stanford University: Pittosporum undulatum

vallisneria-australis.summary: Australian eelgrass, also called ribbon weed, grows underwater with long, strap-shaped leaves rising from the sediment. Runners connect neighboring plants into tall aquatic meadows, while small female flowers reach the surface on slender stalks. After pollination, those stalks coil back underwater, a distinctive feature of its life cycle; despite the common name, this is a freshwater plant rather than a marine seagrass.

sources.label: California Department of Parks and Recreation: Ribbon weed identification

chloris-truncata.summary: Australian fingergrass is also called windmill grass, a fitting name for the long flower spikes radiating from the top of each stem. It is a low, clumping perennial with relatively narrow leaves, and the small florets darken as they mature. Often associated with grassland on heavy soils in its native region, its wheel-shaped seed heads make it easier to recognize than many grasses before flowering.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Chloris truncata
University of Sydney eFlora: Chloris truncata

eragrostis-leptostachya.summary: Australian lovegrass is a slender, tufted perennial with narrow leaves and an open, branching flower head above the foliage. Its small spikelets hold several tightly arranged florets, giving them a finely segmented appearance. Native to eastern and southeastern Australia, it is also known as paddock lovegrass; examining the flower head and the tiny hairs where leaf meets stem helps distinguish it from other similar grasses.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew GrassBase: Eragrostis leptostachya

toona-ciliata.summary: Australian redcedar is a large deciduous rainforest tree with long compound leaves and a broad, spreading crown. Small pale flowers give way to capsules that split open and release winged seeds. Its soft, workable timber made it historically valuable, while prolific seed production can support spread beyond planted trees, so young seedlings deserve as much attention as the impressive mature canopy.

sources.label: Botanic Gardens of Sydney: Australian red cedar

cherax-quadricarinatus.summary: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, often blue-green, with a bright red patch along the outer claw of mature males. It eats a mixture of plant and animal material and is raised commercially in ponds. Its movement through aquaculture has taken it beyond its native range, making escaped or released animals relevant to the ecology of receiving waterways.

sources.label: USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Australian redclaw crayfish
Joyce and colleagues (2016), James Cook University: Redclaw feeding study

atriplex-semibaccata.summary: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading perennial with gray-green leaves that often look dusted or mealy underneath. Small flowers sit in the leaf axils, followed by reddish to mauve structures surrounding the seeds. It can grow on saline soils, dry rocky slopes, and disturbed ground, so its low profile may hide a plant well suited to difficult sites where other vegetation struggles.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Atriplex semibaccata, Flora of Iraq and Flora of Tropical East Africa

leptospermum-laevigatum.summary: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers, and woody seed capsules with flat tops. Older trunks can become strikingly twisted beneath shaggy, fibrous bark, making mature plants quite different in appearance from a clipped hedge. Newer botanical treatments may call it Gaudium laevigatum, so that name can help connect nursery labels and identification references.

sources.label: Stanford University: Australian tea tree

trachymela-sloanei.summary: Australian tortoise beetle is a eucalyptus leaf feeder whose adults and larvae can leave conspicuous notches along leaf edges. The insects often hide on or beneath bark during the day, so the tattered foliage may be easier to spot than its cause. Well-established eucalyptus can tolerate substantial feeding, which makes the condition of the whole tree more informative than a damaged leaf alone.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Eucalyptus tortoise beetles

ficopomatus-enigmaticus.summary: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube and extends a feathery crown into the water to collect food. In sheltered brackish waters, many individuals can build reeflike masses on hard surfaces or over sediment, changing habitat and fouling boats or waterfront structures. Despite its common name, its original geographic home remains uncertain, and large reef formation does not occur everywhere it is found.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Ficopomatus enigmaticus
Smithsonian NEMESIS California: Ficopomatus enigmaticus ecology

cotula-australis.summary: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing herb with finely divided leaves and tiny buttonlike flower heads on slender stalks. The pale yellow or cream flowers lack the showy outer petals of many daisies, so the heads can seem surprisingly plain. It grows in open grassy places and can appear in roadsides and lawns, where its divided foliage is a useful clue before the little flower stalks rise.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Cotula australis

pinus-nigra.summary: Austrian pine is a substantial evergreen with stiff, dark green needles held in pairs and dark, furrowed bark. Young trees tend to be pyramidal, while older crowns become rounded and spreading. Long planted as a screen or windbreak, it tolerates varied soils and some drought once established; paired needles and outward-pointing brown cones offer practical clues when comparing it with other landscape pines.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox: Pinus nigra

rorippa-austriaca.summary: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial with toothed leaves that partly clasp the stem and clusters of small yellow flowers. Its nearly round fruits help distinguish it from mustards with long, narrow seedpods. It grows along periodically flooded riverbanks and other moist, disturbed places, and can spread through underground runners, so a patch may expand even when few well-developed seeds are visible.

sources.label: Burgenland Flora: Rorippa austriaca
